name: Antiperspirant

lead: Antiperspirants keep your underarms dry. That means no sweat marks on shirts, less of the moisture odor-causing bacteria feed on, and a fresher presence through the day.

Aluminium salts react with sweat and form temporary plugs in the sweat ducts, with a mild astringent effect, so less sweat reaches the skin surface. Sweat reduction is measurable, and stronger versions of the same ingredient family are used for excessive sweating. This differs from a deodorant, which targets odor rather than sweat output.

paras: Most people apply a stick, roll-on, spray or gel to clean, dry underarms as part of a daily grooming routine, and often pair it with a deodorant or fragrance. Stronger formulas exist for heavy sweaters. The effect builds with regular use.

Skin irritation is the most common effect, and zirconium-containing products can cause granulomas. The FDA advises people with kidney problems to consult a doctor first. Concerns about breast cancer and Alzheimer's have been studied, and reviews summarized on Wikipedia found no reliable link.

chain: Drier clothes, less odor, fresher presence
angle.text: Antiperspirants cut underarm sweat with aluminium salts, so shirts stay dry and the moisture odor bacteria feed on is reduced. It is the everyday staple of a grooming routine, and the sweat reduction is visible and measurable.

lead: An antiperspirant is a topical product that reduces sweating, most commonly using aluminium salts such as aluminium chlorohydrate. It differs from a deodorant, which targets odor rather than sweat output.[1][2] In the United States antiperspirants are regulated as over-the-counter drugs, whereas deodorants are cosmetics; in the European Union antiperspirants are generally classed as cosmetics.[1][2]

In appearance culture, antiperspirants are used to control wetness, sweat marks and odor. Aluminium salts are thought to form temporary plugs in sweat-gland ducts, reducing the sweat that reaches the skin surface.[1][2] The same ingredient family at higher strengths is used for hyperhidrosis.[3] Public concerns about links to breast cancer and Alzheimer's disease have been examined in studies; reviews summarized by Wikipedia report no reliable evidence of a link.[1][4][5]

paras: Antiperspirants come as sticks, roll-ons, sprays, gels and creams, and are often sold combined with deodorant.[2] Aluminium chlorohydrate and aluminium zirconium compounds are common actives.[1] Wikipedia notes that antiperspirants are often recommended for application at bedtime.[1]

Everdry, introduced in 1903, is cited as the first commercial antiperspirant.[1] Jules Montenier patented the modern formulation in 1941, first used in Stopette spray, and a roll-on applicator marketed as Ban Roll-On appeared in 1952.[1] Gillette's Right Guard was the first aerosol antiperspirant in the early 1960s, and in 1977 the FDA banned an aluminium zirconium aerosol ingredient over inhalation concerns.[1] Grokipedia also describes early use of alum and an early aluminium chloride product, Odorono, but these details come from an AI-generated source and may be unreliable.[2]

Odor arises when skin bacteria break down sweat, particularly apocrine secretions.[1][6] Aluminium salts are said to react with sweat to create gel-like plugs in the ducts and to have a mild astringent effect.[1][2]

Breast cancer: a 2002 case-control study in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute examined antiperspirant use and breast cancer risk,[4] while a 2005 review discussed the hypothesis that aluminium could play a role,[7] and a 2003 study reported an association between earlier diagnosis age and frequent use of antiperspirants and underarm shaving.[8] Wikipedia states the popular claim traces to a 1999 email and that the National Cancer Institute considers the research conflicting.[1]

Alzheimer's disease: early and later epidemiological studies examined aluminium-containing products and dementia risk with differing findings,[9][5] and a 2014 review of 469 studies cited by Wikipedia found little evidence of increased risk.[1] A toxicokinetics review describes food as the primary common source of aluminium exposure.[10]

Skin and other effects: the FDA advises people with kidney dysfunction to consult a doctor before using aluminium antiperspirants; zirconium compounds can cause granulomatous reactions; and aerosols held close to the skin can cause cold burns.[1] Axillary granular parakeratosis is a described skin condition of the underarm.[11]

Human studies concerning antiperspirants in this literature are mostly epidemiological, on breast cancer and Alzheimer's disease associations,[4][8][9][5] plus exposure-assessment and microbiota work.[6] Case-control and cohort findings differ, and the studies are observational. No randomized trial of appearance outcomes is cited here.
